title: Should we still be testing on animals?

turns.speaker: Deniz
turns.text: The new rules phase out animal testing for cosmetics entirely by the end of next year, and for some drug categories after that.

turns.speaker: Hana
turns.text: Cosmetics I'd have banned decades ago. Nobody needs a new mascara badly enough.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: Agreed, and that part's easy. The drug side is where it gets uncomfortable, because the alternatives aren't equivalent yet.

turns.speaker: Deniz
turns.text: Organ-on-a-chip is genuinely impressive, though. You get human tissue responding to a human dose.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: For liver toxicity, yes. For anything systemic, a chip doesn't have a nervous system or an immune response.

turns.speaker: Hana
turns.text: So the honest position is that some of it can go now and some of it can't.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: That's where I am. What I object to is pretending the choice is free.

turns.speaker: Deniz
turns.text: The counter-argument I find hard is the predictive one. Something like nine in ten drugs that pass animal trials still fail in humans.

turns.speaker: Deniz
turns.text: Roughly. So the test we're defending on ethical grounds isn't even a good test.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: That's the strongest thing anyone's said to me on this, honestly. Although the failures we never see are the ones it caught.

turns.speaker: Hana
turns.text: Which is unfalsifiable, to be fair.

turns.speaker: Paul
turns.text: It is. I'd still rather be the person making that argument than the one ignoring it.

points: New rules phase out animal testing for cosmetics next year and for some drug categories later.
All three accept the cosmetics ban readily; the disagreement is about medicines.
Paul argues alternatives are not yet equivalent, since organ-on-a-chip models lack nervous and immune systems.
Deniz's strongest point is predictive failure: roughly nine in ten drugs passing animal trials still fail in humans.
Paul concedes this is the strongest objection, but notes the harms the tests prevented are invisible.
Hana points out that this defence is unfalsifiable, which Paul accepts.
